Cube world: four decisions

Deep Time, 22 October 2026. You moved the world from Petroff-Guyou to a cube. The plan and the study of which map to draw on the cube are both done. Four choices are yours.

  • Waiting on you4 decisionsQ4, the map and the turn, then Q1, the format, Q2, the climate interface and Q3, when to build the wrap engine.
  • MeanwhileUndoableThe coordinator took the study's pick: the world on the conformal cube turned freely, the simulation on its own equal-area cube.
  • In flightLava flows (fix 8); gullies, cliffs and craters (D2, D3, D7); the cube's phase 0.

What is waiting on you

Four decisions. The recommended option is first in each. Answer in the terminal with letters, like "Q4 a, Q1 a, Q2 a, Q3 a", or say "all as recommended". The numbers follow the plan's; Q4 comes first because it is the one a player sees.

Words used below

The cube and its net
The planet drawn on the six faces of a cube, laid out as a cross: four band faces round the middle (F0 to F3) that loop east-west, and one face above and one below F0 (N and S). Each face is 3,840 blocks square on a 16k world.
Conformal
A map that draws shapes true at every point: a round crater stays round. The price is area: some land gets more blocks per km² than other land.
Moser cube
The equal-area cube map: every block covers the same area of planet. The price is shape: circles are drawn as ovals, most near the corners.
τ (tau)
The study's dial between the two: τ 0 is conformal, τ 1 is Moser. The values between are only for comparison.
Corners
The 8 points where three faces meet. The conformal map draws land near a corner far too big, so its corners must sit at sea.
The turn
How the cube sits on the planet. On the polar axis, the poles sit at the centres of faces N and S. Turned freely, the cube is rotated until all 8 corners lie far out at sea.
Stretch
The longest over the shortest width of a small circle as a map draws it. 1.00 is round.
Jacobian
How many planet metres one block step covers, in each direction, at one place. On the conformal map it is one number and one angle, the same every way.

Q4. The map and the turn

Asked because the free turn moves the poles off the face centres. The coordinator took (a) as its call, so work goes on with it until you answer.

  • aRecommendedThe conformal cube, turned freely. You see:mountains, volcanoes and craters in their true shape, with the same steepness every way. North points a different way on each face and turns slowly as you walk; the F3 debug screen will show it. Latitude does not run along the grid, so climate bands cross the faces at a slant, and the band faces do not follow the equator. It costs:land is drawn 0.79 to 1.92 times its true area on the worst of 15 planets, so slopes vary from place to place: up to about 15 % between ranges, 2.8 % over 256 blocks. All 8 corners sit 5.3° (about 70 km) or more out at sea. Each world stores its turn, and mic-climate needs the direction of north (Q2). Fix 6, drawing volcanoes and craters round by hand, is no longer needed.
  • bThe conformal cube, with the pole at most 30° from the centre of face N. You see:true shapes, as in (a). North stays within 30° of -z on the polar face. It costs:land up to 2.05 times its true area on the worst planet; corners at least 4.58° (about 60 km) out at sea.
  • cThe equal-area Moser cube on the polar axis. You see:the poles at the centres of N and S, the equator along the middle of the band faces, north is -z on them. Mountains, volcanoes and craters drawn 1.26 times longer one way than the other (median; up to 1.42): round becomes oval, and slopes are steeper one way. Fix 6 stays, to draw volcanoes and craters round. It costs:nothing in area, which is exact. Corners may sit on or next to land (0.18° from it on the study's planet), which costs Moser little, because its areas stay right there.
(a) Conformal, free turn(b) Conformal, pole within 30°(c) Moser, polar axis
Shapes on land, worst stretch1.02 (true)1.02 (true)1.42 (median 1.26)

In every case the simulation runs on its own Moser cube on the polar axis. Its corners cannot be kept at sea, because continents drift over every point in 1,000 Myr. On the conformal map the simulation's corner cells would be tiny, 0.044 of the mean area, so its diffusion steps would have to be 31 times shorter. Moser's corner cell is 0.91 of the mean. The bake carries each world block to the simulation through its place on the planet, whatever the world's map.

Q1. The world-data format 0.7 a data format

Nothing a player sees. It sets how a cube world is stored and which builds can open it.

  • aRecommendedStore the rasters face by face, with no empty cells. Ship the map's table in the code (Rust, the jar and the viewer); each world names its map and the table's hash. It costs:a build with a different table refuses the world, so a new table means new worlds. Before a public release old worlds need not open anyway.
  • bStore the rasters over the cross's whole box (4 by 3 faces), with empty cells where no face is. It costs:simpler for some tools, but every raster takes twice the disk and memory.
  • cCarry the table inside every world. It costs:each world stands alone but is larger, and Rust, Java and JavaScript must all read the table from the world.

Q2. Climate API 5 the interface mic-climate reads

Players see it through mic-climate's seasons and temperatures, which need the latitude at each block. Either way, mic-climate's owner adds "cube" to its PlanetLatitude.

  • aRecommendedKeep the four calls and add two. Keep latitudeDeg, longitudeDeg, projectionKind (new value "cube") and circumferenceBlocks (now the east-west loop, 15,360 blocks on a 16k world). Add northBearingDeg(level, x, z), the direction of north at a block, and metresPerBlock(level, x, z), the local scale. Delete the old latitudeDeg(z, C), which only works on today's flat Lambert world. It costs:two more calls to keep working.
  • bOnly the new kind value, no new calls. It costs:mic-climate gets latitude but not north or the scale. Anything there that needs either works it out itself or does without.

Q3. When to build the wrap engine big scope

The wrap engine joins the cube's edges that turn, so you walk straight across onto the next face. It exists today behind a developer switch. Until it joins the world, those edges are borders: 12 edges of 3,840 blocks, 46,080 blocks in all on a 16k world, with today's rules (the border 1 block inside the edge, a 24-block warning band). Every point stays reachable on foot through F0, both poles included; on Petroff-Guyou the poles sat on borders. The longest walk round a border is 7,680 blocks on a quarter-turn edge and about 10,000 on a half-turn edge; Petroff-Guyou's worst today is 6,656. Building the engine later changes no terrain.

  • aRecommendedAfter V1 (the first version players get) ships on borders. V1 is complete without it.
  • bNow, beside V1. It needs eight work items: the topology, block entities, world generation, entities, the client's view across a turn, the other mods (Toroidal World, Distant Horizons, Sable's ships, Create trains), hardening, and the detail noise. It shares the agents and the test VM with V1's work.
  • cAfter the public release. The first public players get borders.

What the coordinator already decided meanwhile

All undoable before a public release, under your rule of 16 October. Each is in the decisions log of 22 October.

The map

  • The world takes the conformal cube, turned freely: a search turns the cube until its 8 corners lie as far from land as they can. Then the cube's symmetry puts the north pole in face N and the most land on F0. Each world stores the turn.
  • The simulation and the climate grid take their own equal-area Moser cube on the polar axis.
  • Fix 6 (D1, drawing volcanoes and craters round) is dropped: the conformal map draws them round already.
  • Phase 0 commits both maps' tables, so moving to (b) or (c) is a change of data and of one search setting. The fallbacks, in order: (b), then (c).

The layout

  • The cross net: F0 to F3 round the middle, looping east-west through Toroidal World (the mod that loops the world), with N and S on F0. F0 is centred on x = 0.
  • Today's blocks per km². A face is 3,840 blocks on a 16k world, 7,424 on a 32k world and 1,024 on the 4k test planet, rounded to 256. Land comes out at about 310 m per block, against the planet's average of 294.6 m, so slopes are about 5 % steeper.
  • Metres convert to blocks with the local scale everywhere: 213 to 331 m per block on land on the worst planet.
  • Detail noise stays sampled at the world block, as today, blended across the edges that turn.
  • Spawn is at least 256 blocks from any corner.
  • Until the wrap engine, the generator draws the next face, turned, beyond each open edge, behind a border 1 block inside the 12 open edges.

The simulation and the tools

  • The timelapse pictures on the Create World screen stay today's flat pictures of the whole planet.
  • Per-cell climate (P1-26) lands on today's flat grid first and moves with the simulation.
  • The lava-flow paint (fix 8) lands in the game as built; phase 2 carries its walk across the faces' edges.
  • Phase 0 started on the older equal-area table and swaps in the study's tables.
  • PLT-400 is on in every preset, landed with D6: a collision's wedge of crust crosses whole.

Play and clean-up

  • The fresh multiplayer world (D5) goes ahead on Petroff-Guyou. Its build is tagged play-d5 for hotfixes.
  • The cube's play world waits for both phase 2 (the game on the cube) and phase 4 (the simulation on the cube), so players get one more fresh world, not two.
  • Today's Lambert and Petroff-Guyou world shapes and an earlier trial map (the quincuncial prototype) are deleted when phase 2 lands; the flat simulation grid when phase 4 lands.

The evidence for the map

The projection study measured the maps on 15 baked planets: test runs and worlds you have played. The pictures and the slope numbers come from one of them, a quick 16k planet after 1,000 Myr, called "this planet" below. Nothing has been checked in game yet.

Three mountain ranges, four ways

Each panel is 1,024 by 1,024 blocks of shaded relief round one range. The white rings are 50 and 150 km from its centre: true circles, so how a map draws them shows what it does to shapes.

High latitude: 62.6° N, 267.0° E

The highest of the three, 5,761 m on average within 25 km of the centre. Today's map squeezes the 150 km ring into an oval about 2.3 to 1. The conformal cube draws it round, and a little larger than true, because land there gets more blocks than average. Moser draws it about 1.2 to 1. The cube panels are turned against the true shape: the freely turned cube puts north a different way at each place.

Mid latitude: 38.7° N, 249.7° E

4,810 m on average within 25 km. Today's map draws the rings as wide ovals; the conformal cube draws them round; Moser nearly round. The small arrow at the centre points north: up in the true shape, to the right on both cubes here. That is the free turn.

Low latitude: 10.9° S, 339.0° E

4,739 m on average within 25 km. Today's map draws the rings as tall ovals, so the range looks thin. The conformal cube draws them round. Moser draws a visible oval.

The fine streaks running one way in every panel, the true shape included, are the simulation's grain: erosion is carved on today's flat simulation grid, whose cells stretch away from the equator. They go when the simulation moves to its own cube (phase 4), whichever map the world takes.

The same three ranges from the side

A low view of each range, looking from the bottom edge of its panel above. Because the cube is turned, each cube map shows the range from a different side than today's map does.

This planet's land on the cross net. Brown is mountain land (1 km up or more), green the rest. The lines show blocks per planet area: 1.00 is the average, 2.00 means land there is drawn twice its true size. The rings round each corner climb past 2.00.

The smallest distance from the 8 corners to land, in degrees of the planet (about 14 km a degree on this planet). Negative means a corner on land.

How big land is drawn

The worst land on each planet, as one factor: how many times too big or too small, whichever is worse. The worst of 15 planets, with the median planet below it.

Moser's 1.67 and 1.02 are its table's error where a corner sits on or near land; the map itself is exact. Pole within 10° and 20° fall between the polar axis and 30° (conformal: 2.63 and 2.57); τ 0.25, 0.625 and 0.875 fall between their neighbours. Only τ 0 and τ 1 are on offer: the maps between are the study's own construction, need a scale for every direction at every place, as Moser does, and still need the free turn.

Slopes, between places and by direction

Blocks are 35 m tall, so a slope is drawn steeper by the horizontal metres per block over 35: 8.42 times at the planet's average of 294.6 m per block. A map that varies area changes that from place to place. A map that stretches shapes changes it by direction, at one place. This planet's mountain land, free turn:

MapSteeper byBetween placesBy directionOver 256 blocks
Conformal options a, b8.838.15 to 9.371.15max 1.421.00max 1.022.8 %
τ 0.58.628.28 to 8.861.07max 1.201.12max 1.201.3 %
τ 0.758.528.35 to 8.631.03max 1.101.19max 1.300.6 %
Moser option c8.42all over1.001.26max 1.420
Today Petroff-Guyou8.42all over1.001.49max 2.640

Steeper by: how many times steeper than true a slope is drawn, median, with the 5th to 95th percentile below. Between places: the 95th percentile of that over the 5th, with the largest over the smallest below. By direction: at one place, the steepest way over the gentlest, median and largest. Over 256 blocks: how much the scale changes over 256 blocks, median. On today's map the steepest way is drawn 10.3 times steeper and the gentlest 6.9 (medians).

Every cube map spreads slopes over about the same total, 1.34 to 1.42 from the steepest drawn to the gentlest. They differ in where the spread goes:

  • Within one place, a player sees it in a single view: a round crater drawn as an oval, slopes facing one way steeper than those at right angles. You asked for that to be corrected on Petroff-Guyou (D1, fix 6).
  • Between places, it hides. The conformal map changes the scale by 2.8 % over 256 blocks (about 75 km), the same every way. True slopes on mountain land already vary 2.9 times between the median (3.8°) and the 90th percentile (11.1°).

A local vertical scale could remove even the between-place spread on the conformal map (27.7 to 39.3 m per block on this planet's mountains), but every height conversion would then need the local scale. Not recommended for now.

What makes mountains weak today

Two causes are maps, and the cube fixes both. Three are not maps, and no map fixes them.

Optional 1Report the load failure to Project Atmosphere?

Project Atmosphere fails to load if Remove Reloading Screen is set to hide all overlays. The pack's setting avoids it, so nothing is broken for you. A report would come from you.

Optional 2Keep the agents' lower CPU weight after a reboot?

Background agents get a fifth of the CPU weight they had, until the next reboot. Keeping it means a change to your NixOS config.
